title: supermarket/products
description: One row per distinct product line carried by the chain. The catalogue. Every product has a scannable EAN-13 barcode, a category, a supplier and a shelf price. This is the anchor table for anything to do with what the shop sells.

id.description: Surrogate primary key, sequential from 1. Use this for joins rather than the SKU or the barcode.

sku.description: Internal stock-keeping unit. The chain's own reference, used on shelf labels and in ordering.

ean13.description: The printed barcode, thirteen digits with a correct check digit -- so a barcode library will actually decode it instead of rejecting it. The leading 84 is the GS1 country prefix for Spain.

name.description: Shelf name in Spanish: what the product is, the brand, and the pack size, exactly as a price label would read.
examples: Aceite de oliva virgen extra Campo Sur 1L

category_id.description: The shelf this product sits on. Always a level-2 category, never a top-level aisle.

supplier_id.description: Who the chain buys this product from. One supplier per product line.

brand.description: Own-brand or supplier brand name. All sixteen are invented and none corresponds to a real grocery brand.

unit.description: How the product is sold: by the item (ud), by weight (kg), by volume (L) or as a multipack. This determines whether a quantity can be fractional.

unit_price.description: Shelf price including VAT, in euros. Prices end in .99, .95 or .49 far more often than chance, because retailers really do price that way.

cost_price.description: What the chain pays the supplier per unit. Always below unit_price, giving a gross margin between about 12% and 45% depending on category.

vat_rate.description: Spanish VAT band applied at the till, inherited from the product's category. One of 0.04, 0.10 or 0.21.

active.description: Whether the line is still listed. Roughly 7% are discontinued but retained for historical sales, which is exactly why old transactions can still reference them.
